28b9b2d821.a: Dr. Awua-Larbi was volunteering in the emergency room with a friend when she began transporting patients from the ER to imaging. While transporting them, she started having conversations with patients about their lives and families rather than just their medical conditions. She felt comfortable in that setting and realized it was the human connection that drew her to medicine. After that experience, she went to her advisor and said she knew exactly what she wanted to do: become a doctor based on her appreciation for the human connection in clinical settings.

ff2380fd28.q: What is the core message of Dr. Stella Awua-Larbi's book 'The Other Side of the Bed'?
ff2380fd28.a: The book's core message is that minimizing labeling is essential because you cannot discover someone through a label. While labeling can feel protective, it restricts the whole life underneath that label. Dr. Awua-Larbi emphasizes that the principles apply across humanity—in education, caregiving, and personal relationships. The book uses hospital-based cases and her own clinical experience, but ultimately the message is for all of humanity: understanding that behind every label or medical chart there is a human story that explains not only attitude but also physical and mental status.

When she turned 50, she set a specific goal to do something purposeful beyond her daily physician work and share her experiences. She woke up very early in the morning and dedicated 30 minutes to one hour after work consistently starting in the fall, using the already-collected stories as her foundation. 5e2887a578.a: Dr. Awua-Larbi's self-care is a small quiet room or prayer room that fits only a two-seater couch, decorated with pink artificial flowers and a small lamp. She has set a boundary where her family knows not to disturb her when she enters this space. She spends 15 to 30 minutes or longer sitting, praying, listening to music that speaks to her heart, or simply being quiet. The room has two Bible verses on the wall—'Be still and know I'm God' and another about not being anxious—which remind her that everything will be okay.
